title: Jesus Prays for Himself, His Disciples, and All Believers
summary: At the end of the farewell discourse Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays. He asks the Father to glorify the Son in the hour that has come, then prays for his disciples, that the Father would protect them in the world, keep them from the evil one, and sanctify them by the truth. Finally he prays for all who will believe through their message, that they may be one as the Father and the Son are one, and that they may be with him to see his glory.
story: Chapters 13 to 16 were Jesus speaking to his disciples; chapter 17 is Jesus speaking to his Father, with the disciples listening. It is the longest recorded prayer of Jesus and the climax of the Upper Room Discourse. Immediately after it, in chapter 18, Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley to the garden where he will be arrested. So this prayer stands at the threshold of the passion: it is Jesus' own account of what he has done and what he is about to do. The hour that had not yet come in chapters 2, 7, and 8 has now arrived (17:1). Everything Jesus has taught about the Father, the world, love, truth, and glory is gathered up here and offered back to God.
historical:
The prayer is spoken in Jerusalem at Passover, on the night before Jesus' crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea from about AD 26 to 36. Since the sixteenth century it has often been called Jesus' High Priestly Prayer, a name frequently traced to the Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus, though the idea of Jesus as priest in this chapter is much older. The title reflects a real pattern. On the Day of Atonement, Israel's high priest made atonement first for himself and his household and then for the whole assembly of Israel (Leviticus 16:6, 17). Jesus prays first concerning himself, then for his disciples, then for all who will believe, and he speaks of sanctifying himself for them (17:19), language used of priests and sacrifices set apart for God.

The prayer looks beyond the first disciples to “those who will believe in Me through their message” (17:20), which includes John's first readers late in the first century and every generation since. By then the church included Jews and Gentiles across the Roman world, and questions of unity between them were pressing, as Paul's letters show.
cultural:
Jesus prays standing and looking up to heaven (17:1), a common Jewish posture of prayer (compare 11:41; Mark 7:34), rather than kneeling or bowing. He addresses God simply as Father, as he does throughout John, and also as Holy Father (17:11) and Righteous Father (17:25). Jewish prayer often began by blessing or naming God's character, and these titles do the same.

In the Bible a person's name stands for their character, reputation, and presence. God put his name on the temple in Jerusalem as the place where he would dwell (Deuteronomy 12:11; 1 Kings 8:29). When Jesus says he has revealed the Father's name to the disciples (17:6, 26) and asks the Father to protect them by his name (17:11), he means that he has made God himself known, and that God's own character and power will keep them. To sanctify (17:17, 19) means to set apart as holy for God's use, as priests, sacrifices, and the temple were set apart in Israel.
literary: The prayer has three movements, marked by whom Jesus prays for: himself and his glory (17:1-5), the disciples he is leaving in the world (17:6-19), and all future believers (17:20-26). Repeated words bind it: the world (eighteen times), give (the Father gives the Son authority, people, words, and glory), glory and glorify, name, know, and one. The prayer uses the same circular, layered style as the discourse, where each petition returns to earlier themes with new depth. Its language often sounds like a summary of the Gospel: eternal life, the hour, the work the Father gave, the Son sent into the world, the disciples sent in turn. It ends not with a request but with a promise that Jesus will continue to make the Father's name known (17:26).

outline.t: Jesus prays for his own glorification
Jesus prays for all who will believe

doctrines.note: Jesus speaks of “the glory I had with You before the world existed” (17:5) and of the Father's love for him “before the foundation of the world” (17:24). The Son's relationship with the Father did not begin at his birth; it is eternal. The unity of Father and Son is the pattern for the unity of believers (17:21-22).

“Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent” (17:3). Eternal life is not only endless time but a quality of life: knowing God personally through the Son. It begins now and continues forever.

Jesus prays that believers may be one, “so that the world may believe that You sent Me” (17:21). The unity of Christians is part of their witness. The prayer has long been central to efforts toward Christian unity, and it stands as a judgment on the church's divisions.

Here Jesus intercedes for his people, and the New Testament presents him as continuing to intercede for them after his ascension (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). The prayer also shows the content of Jesus' concern for his followers: protection, holiness, joy, unity, and his presence.

words.note: Doxazō, to glorify. The prayer opens, “Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You” (17:1). In John the Son is glorified through the cross, resurrection, and return to the Father, where the Father's love and faithfulness are shown in full. The glory he asks for is the glory he had with the Father before creation (17:5).

Hagiazō, to sanctify or make holy, to set apart for God. Jesus asks the Father to sanctify the disciples by the truth, God's word (17:17), and says he sanctifies himself for them (17:19). Many interpreters hear sacrificial language: Jesus consecrates himself to die, so that his people may be set apart for God.

Tēreō, to keep, guard, or protect. Jesus has kept the disciples while with them and asks the Father to keep them now, both by his name and from the evil one (17:11-12, 15). He does not ask that they be taken out of the world, but that they be guarded in it.

Apōleia, destruction or perdition. Judas is called “the son of destruction” (17:12), a Hebrew-style expression meaning one who belongs to or is destined for destruction. Paul uses the same phrase in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 of the figure of lawlessness.

christ: This chapter lets the reader overhear the Son speaking with the Father on the eve of the cross. It shows the eternal fellowship of Father and Son, the glory they shared before creation, and the Son's complete confidence that he has finished the work he was given (17:4). It shows Jesus as the great high priest, consecrating himself as the sacrifice and interceding for his people, which the letter to the Hebrews will develop at length. And it shows the goal of his work: that people from every generation may know the only true God, be one in his love, and be with Jesus to see his glory. The prayer is still being answered.

hard.q: If Judas was lost “so that the Scripture would be fulfilled,” did he have any choice?
hard.a:
Jesus says none of the disciples was lost except the son of destruction, “so that the Scripture would be fulfilled” (17:12), probably referring to Psalm 41:9, quoted in 13:18. Readers naturally ask whether Judas was fated to betray. Christian traditions answer differently. Augustinian and Reformed interpreters hold that God ordained the betrayal within his sovereign plan while Judas acted freely and bore full guilt, in the same way that Acts 2:23 speaks of Jesus being handed over by God's set purpose and by the hands of lawless men. Arminian and many other interpreters hold that God foreknew what Judas would freely choose and that Scripture foretold it without causing it. Some stress that the psalm describes a pattern of the righteous sufferer betrayed by a friend, which Judas fulfilled by his own choices.

The Gospels themselves treat Judas as responsible. John describes his theft (12:6) and the devil's influence (13:2, 27), yet Jesus washes his feet and offers him the morsel, gestures of love to the end. How God's purposes and human freedom fit together is a mystery the Bible affirms from both sides without fully explaining.

questions: Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God. How does that change what you expect eternal life to be?
Jesus prays that his followers would not be taken out of the world but kept in it. How do you tend to respond to the world: by withdrawing, by blending in, or by being sent?
Jesus prays that believers would be one so the world may believe. What is one step you could take toward unity with Christians unlike you?
